prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of the optical lattice clock, in which atoms trapped at a magic wavelength allow frequency measurement at the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged from round 1: B041 as a single part for Katori and Ye. The scientific core is specific and checkable. Katori's magic-wavelength lattice removes the light shift so that thousands of atoms can be interrogated at once without Doppler or recoil penalties, and the strontium and ytterbium-type realisations, above all Ye's work at JILA, took systematic uncertainty and stability to the 10^-18 range. What persuades me most as a theorist embedded in experimental teams is that the result is not one group's claim: JILA, Tokyo/RIKEN, PTB, NIST, SYRTE and others run and compare these clocks, and the many-body coherence and millimetre-scale redshift measurements are visible in the data. The chair's first question asks for a citation that names the lattice concept and the record-level realisation without implying that NIST, PTB and SYRTE did nothing. I propose exactly that wording: it credits the invention and its development, and says nothing about all optical clocks, so it is separated from the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion-control prize while leaving accuracy-evaluation work by others unclaimed rather than denied. I deliberately do not put 'fundamental physics' in the citation any more, because constant-variation and dark-matter results are so far null and the prize should reward what has been demonstrated.
statement.case_against: The honest weakness is that this is a measurement achievement, and a committee that wants a newly discovered phenomenon in nature can say so; I think the answer is that the lattice clock opened a regime (many-body clock physics, interrogation of thousands of atoms at once, centimetre and millimetre redshift) that single-ion clocks could not reach, but I accept that this is a judgment and not a proof. The priority picture is also not perfectly clean: Lemonde, Takamoto, Derevianko, Ludlow and the NIST, PTB and SYRTE groups made real contributions to the concept and to accuracy evaluation, and a two-name prize cannot reflect them. Finally, the redefinition of the second is still pending, so part of the downstream payoff is still ahead of us. None of this, in my view, outweighs the maturity and reproducibility of the result, but a member who weights novelty over maturity is not being unreasonable.

responses.point: Ulf prefers B004 (Kane, Mele, Molenkamp) as the discovery with the clearest before and after, and asks whether his scepticism about the lattice clock rests on it being a refinement of measurement rather than a new quantum phenomenon; he concedes the 2016 topological prize is close and that Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang and Hasan sit outside the three names.
responses.response: I take your before-and-after test seriously and I think the clock passes it: before, trapped-atom spectroscopy was limited to a few atoms and light shifts, and after it, large ensembles reach 10^-18 and resolve gravitational redshift over millimetres, which is a regime change and not a polish. On B004 I defer to you and the condensed-matter members on the science, but your own file lists the two obstacles that worry me most, a 2016 prize that sits very close in lineage and a credit that omits the people who proposed the HgTe realisation. The clock has neither problem, which is why I would ask you, in answer to the chair, whether those two concessions are not already the reason to move your first choice toward B041, which you already list as an alternative. I would not call this a settled disagreement about discovery versus instrument; I would accept that a precision prize is a legitimate kind of discovery when it opens measurements nobody could make.

responses.point: Olle prefers B017 with a three-name credit (MacDonald, Jarillo-Herrero, Bistritzer), arguing that independent reproduction and moire follow-ups show lasting impact, and he says optical lattice clocks have unquestionable maturity and that he may be weighting his own field too generously.
responses.response: Your answer to my round-1 question is useful: you treat the existence of correlated insulating and superconducting phases as the discovery and not the pairing mechanism, and the high-Tc analogy is fair. I remain unpersuaded for this year, not because the science is weak but because the phase diagram, the role of strain and disorder, and the superconducting mechanism are still moving, and a prize citation cannot be written without choosing among interpretations. You also write that the clock's maturity is unquestionable, and I would take that at face value: your reservation on B041 was novelty relative to 2005 and 2012, and I hope the citation I propose, which names the magic-wavelength lattice rather than optical clocks in general, answers it. I appreciate your suggestion that I should not lead on circuit QED; I will not, and I note I have given up B028 as my preferred prize for this reason and for the 2025 timing you raise, though I do not agree with the implication that the science is lesser.

responses.point: Bernhard prefers B027 (Young, Halperin, Nelson) as a mature, analytically controlled theory with clean authorship of the decisive papers, and lists B041 first among his alternatives, saying he would accept it as the likely consensus.
responses.response: I respect the clarity of the KTHNY mechanism and the fact that the authorship is as clean as it gets for a theory prize, and as a theorist I share your taste for compact, general mechanisms. My hesitation is the one you list yourself: the 2016 prize rewarded defect-driven phase transitions, and you concede that real 2D systems melt first order in some cases, so the claim of universality is not borne out everywhere. Colloid and simulation work that tested the hexatic phase is also not among the credited names, so the experimental confirmation that the chair asks for is not in the configuration. Given that you already accept B041 as a likely consensus, I would ask whether you would support the citation I propose, which rests the prize on the lattice invention and its realisation rather than on a general-purpose claim about precision measurement.

responses.point: Eva Lindroth supports B041 and wants a citation that names the lattice and the 10^-18 level, mentions Lemonde, Takamoto and Derevianko as having claims on specific steps, and notes that constant-variation results so far are null.
responses.response: We agree that the citation should lead with the clocks and not with fundamental physics, and I have dropped that phrase from my wording. On the credit, your point that Lemonde, Takamoto and Derevianko have claims on distinct steps (shift theory, early demonstrations, comparisons) matters most. I would answer the chair's question by deliberately limiting the citation to the invention and development of the lattice clock, so that the committee's own background text, and not the citation, records the contribution of the NIST, PTB and SYRTE groups. I also thank you for the earlier remark that Cirac and Zoller are a less urgent call because the experimental side was honoured in 2012; on reflection I accept that this weakens the case for B002 as a second part this year, and I now treat B002 only as an alternative.

responses.point: Stefan supports B041, asks that the citation name the magic-wavelength lattice explicitly, and says my opening B028 support should be counted as recusal.
responses.response: I accept your suggestion on both points. The wording I propose names the lattice and the magic wavelength explicitly, which is also what Eva Olsson asks for, and I agree that my opening ranking of B028 should be discounted and that I should not argue for it. Your remark that the support for B041 comes from members with different specialties, not only from atomic physicists, is the reason I trust it more than any single-subfield favourite, and I would not want a recusal on my side to be read as pushing the committee toward circuit QED later.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will accept a precision-measurement achievement as the prize-worthy discovery when the fundamental-physics payoffs (varying constants, dark matter, a redefined second) are not yet delivered.

Whether the citation wording can name the lattice concept and its record-level realisations without a priority dispute with Lemonde, Takamoto, Derevianko and the NIST, PTB and SYRTE groups; I am relying on colleagues in atomic physics for the fine priority chronology.

Whether circuit QED (B028) would be the better prize in a future year once the 2025 recognition is further in the past and the Blais allocation is settled; I am not in a position to argue that case this year.
Whether any second part is worth adding, since B041 takes two of the three allowed names and any second achievement would need to be credited to a single person.
statement.conflict_note: I lead the Wallenberg Centre for Quantum Technology and work closely with superconducting-qubit groups at Chalmers, and circuit and waveguide QED is directly adjacent to the credited B028 candidates. In response to the chair, I treat my opening first-place ranking of B028 as discounted, I will not argue for B028 or B002 in this round, and I would recuse myself from any final decision on B028 if it came to a vote. Eva Olsson, Bernhard Mehlig and I share the Chalmers environment without any specific collaboration that I am aware of, and I have no known tie to Katori, Ye or the other B041 names. I have no specific conflict with the other shortlisted candidates from my profile.
